name: Pomp and Circumstance
description:
There is always more to a musician than just their music. 
This talk uncovers the life of Harikeshanallur Dr. L. Muthiah Bhagavatar (1877–1945), a flamboyant and larger-than-life figure who found joy in every form of expression available to him. He was a renowned musician, a prolific composer, a consummate Harikatha performer, a well-regarded teacher, and the author of a treatise on Carnatic music theory. 
Trained first as a Carnatic musician, Bhagavatar soon turned to Harikatha, finding in its blend of storytelling, song, and stagecraft a fuller outlet for his gifts, quickly becoming one of its most popular exponents. As an important figure at the Mysore court, under the patronage of King Krishnaraja Wodeyar, he composed one hundred and eight songs in praise of Goddess Chamundi, each one a fresh attempt at devotion. At the invitation of Maharani Sethu Parvathy Bai, he later moved to the Travancore Palace, where he became the first principal of the Trivandrum Music College, turning his private joy in music into a public institution for teaching it. 
Even scholarship, for Bhagavatar, became another register of expression. He was the first musician to be awarded a doctorate, for his thesis, Sangita Kalpadrumam. Published only after his death, his theoretical work was born of the same curiosity that drove his performances. Across his lifetime he composed more than four hundred songs in multiple languages and introduced around twenty new ragas into the Carnatic tradition. In 1920, he founded a gurukula, the Tyagaraja Sangita Vidyalaya, in Madurai, ensuring that this capacity for joyful reinvention would outlive him, carried forward by students such as Madurai Mani Iyer.

name: Can Data Transform Indian Agriculture?
description:
Farming has always been based on reading data: the rhythm of seasons, the cycles of rain, the subtle signs a landscape gives before it fails. Water, more than any other signal, has long determined success or failure. This panel explores how remote sensing and ground-collected data can offer early indicators of landscape health, flagging agricultural challenges before they escalate. 
Bringing together voices from research, government, and technology, the panel asks what unlocking water data, in all its old and new forms, could mean for the future of Indian agriculture. What possibilities remain untapped in the data already available, and what other sources might still be unlocked?

name: The Day the Chariot Moved
description:
There is an India hiding in plain sight, asking us to pull the chariot. 
Mindtree co-founder Subroto Bagchi returns to BIC, where he spoke in 2006 at one of the earliest programmes, to chart how his idea of the entrepreneur has changed across twenty years. What does “entrepreneur” mean once you meet the people who truly keep the world moving? 
After four decades in the corporate sector, he answered Chief Minister Naveen Patnaik’s call to work with the Government of Odisha, spending eight years there largely on skill development. In this talk, he will explore a new version of the economy, one built at the grassroots rather than in boardrooms. He will introduce the nano unicorns: ordinary people in small towns, given training and a small grant to build what they see as necessary. He will make the case that skill development is not merely a route to employability but an instrument of human transformation. 
This talk is part of a series marking twenty years of BIC, in which speakers and artists from the institution’s early years return to revisit the topics they first addressed. Each session traces what has changed, what has endured, and what to make of the same topics two decades on.

name: The Unknown Mahatmas Who Made the Mahatma
description:
We know the freedom struggle’s great names, its fighters, and its stars. But there are many more influences that often get lost in the stories. This performance traces the people Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi met along his journey: the lesser-known encounters, quiet and easily overlooked, who helped turn him into the great man history remembers. 
Through song, anecdote, and lore, the performance unpacks the word itself. Mahatma. It asks what this title might still mean today, in a world so far removed from the one that first gave it to him. What does it really take to turn a man into a Mahatma?

name: Beyond the Buzz
description:
This panel discussion examines India’s relationship with alcohol, from its colonial history to the current state of the industry, and how deeply its marketing is rooted in that history. Panelists will trace how colonial rule promoted distillery-based alcohol production to extract revenue for the empire, and how those same patterns continue to shape how alcohol is sold and consumed today. What does a drink marketed as celebration, sophistication, even heart health, carry behind the glamour? 
Though direct advertising is banned in India, the liquor industry remains worth an estimated sixty-five billion dollars, sustained instead through aspiration, imagery, and social pressure. Recent research suggests that between twenty-five and forty percent of Indian drinkers qualify as hazardous or dependent drinkers, a gap the panel will contextualise through the lived and professional experience of its speakers, who bring perspectives as mental health practitioners and individuals with firsthand experience of addiction. Changing the image of alcohol as an essential ingredient of celebration, the panel argues, may be one of the most consequential shifts available to public health today.

name: The Many Pasts of Panipat, 1761
description:
A great “what if?” moment in Indian history, the Third Battle of Panipat in 1761 has produced martyrs, ballads, and endless partisan debate. This lecture examines how its retelling, across school textbooks, Hindu nationalist historiography, and cinema, has flattened a complex event into a tale of heroes and villains. It raises the question, whose Panipat are we really remembering? 
The vernacular primary sources tell a different story: where popular memory insists on certainty, they equivocate, contradict, and complicate. A micro history of the battle reveals multiple pasts, remembered and recorded by multiple men. This lecture makes a case for why critical historians cannot ignore this plurality while narrating the event to a generation raised on a communal rendering of Indian history. 
About Satish Chandra 
Professor Satish Chandra (1922-2017) was one of India’s foremost historians and a towering authority on medieval Indian history. Over a distinguished four-decade career, he taught at leading universities across the country, including Allahabad University, Aligarh Muslim University, Delhi University, Rajasthan University, and finally Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU). At JNU, he co-founded the Centre for Historical Studies alongside S. Gopal, Bipin Chandra, and Romila Thapar. As Chairman of the University Grants Commission, he went on to help shape academic life across India, and in 1985, deeply committed to intellectual exchange, he co-founded the Society for Indian Ocean Studies. A thoughtful historian who brought a Marxist approach to the field, Chandra’s work bridged eras and ideas, leaving an enduring mark on the study of India’s past.

Alok Chandra

name: South India's Forgotten Decade of War
description:
The Nawab of Arcot was a highly coveted title in the mid-eigthteenth century Deccan, resulting in a struggle known as the Carnatic Wars. This discussion will explore how it laid the foundations of the British empire and altered the political course of the Indian subcontinent. 
The Carnatic Wars ran for decades, between local factions backed by the French and English trading companies. The military lessons learned during the conflicts at Arcot, Cuddalore, Pondicherry and Trichy were then applied by the English in their campaigns across the Indian subcontinent. This session offers a unique take on reading history, sans judgement, with an open mind and compassion for the human beings behind the famous names.

name: Echoes of the Earth
description:
65 min | English with subtitles | India | Ganesh Shankar Raj 
Echoes of the Earth: Indigenous Knowledge and Climate Resilience in Karnataka and Kerala explores how traditional knowledge, shaped by centuries of observation, can build climate resilience and nurture a careful, sustainable relationship with the environment. 
Through personal stories and intimate portraits of everyday life, the film highlights practices that conserve forests, biodiversity and natural resources. It also reflects on how climate change is already affecting plants, wildlife and ecosystems, particularly among the Soliga communities of Karnataka. What can these knowledge systems teach us about living sustainably, and what might be overlooked when their ecological dimensions are viewed mainly through cultural or religious traditions? 
The screening will be followed by a panel discussion on the role of Indigenous women as knowledge holders and contributors to environmental stewardship. Indigenous knowledge is not only a legacy of the past, but a living resource for building climate resilience today.

name: Little Language Film Festival
description:
Languages carry more than words. They hold songs, stories, myths, proverbs, poetry and the lived experiences of the communities that speak them. This film festival is more than a celebration of linguistic diversity. It is a reminder of what is at stake when a language disappears: an entire perspective and expression of the world. 
Across India, languages such as Tiwa, Kodava, Santhali, Kurmali, Kokborok and Sherdukpen are spoken by communities whose linguistic traditions are increasingly vulnerable. Globalisation and the dominance of economically powerful languages have accelerated this process, putting many lesser-spoken languages at risk of disappearing. This film festival brings together films in some of these near-forgotten languages, offering an opportunity to encounter their speakers, stories and worlds on their own terms. 
Alongside the screenings, the festival will bring together filmmakers, writers and others working with endangered languages for a conversation on their importance, impact and inheritance. 
Schedule 
Day 1 | Oct 10 | 11:30am – 5:30pm 
11:30am – 11:45am: Opening Note 
11:45am – 1:30pm: Sikaisal / If Only Trees Could Talk
104 minutes | Tiwa with English subtitles | 2022 | Bobby Sarma Baruah
Directed by Bobby Sarma Baruah, Sikaisal won the NFA for Best Film in Tiwa language. It is based on the real-life struggles of Maheshwar Patar, a dedicated school teacher in Ulukunchi village of Assam. It highlights his determination to educate children in a remote community of North East India in the face of countless challenges. The film also won a Special Jury Mention at the 28th Kolkata IFF. 
1:30pm – 3pm: Break 
3pm – 5:30pm: Kherwal
125 minutes | Santali with English subtitles | 2023 | Uttam Kamati
An acclaimed Santhali language film, Kherwal is directed and produced by Uttam Kamati. After the sudden death of the Norwegian Samuel, an academic Padre who was researching their tribal culture, Bidu strives to fulfill the Padre’s last wish: to be buried in the village. This sets off a poignant journey for Bidu’s young son, who is devastated as he wanted to travel to Norway with the academic. Kherwal uniquely features non-professional actors, including a local mobile repair shop owner as the lead character. The film has been celebrated on the festival circuit, winning awards at the Jaipur IFF and the IFF of Kerala. 
The screening will be followed by an audience Q&A. 
Day 2 | Oct 11 | 11:30am – 7pm 
11:30am – 1pm: Panel discussion on Endangered Languages
A conversation on the importance of endangered languages and the cultural worlds they hold. Filmmakers, writers and practitioners reflect on the challenges faced by lesser-spoken languages, and the ways in which they can be documented, nurtured and kept alive. 
1pm – 2pm: Break 
2pm – 4:30pm: Ber / The Root
125 minutes | Kodava with English subtitles | 2023 | Prakash Kariappa
Ber was written, directed and produced by ex-service man Prakash Kariappa. The Kodava language film encapsulates the intricacies of a father-daughter relationship and in the process delves into themes of tradition, generational divides, and the need to preserve the Kodava culture. It has featured in festivals including BIFFes and Dhaka International Film Festival. 
The screening will be followed by an audience Q&A. 
4:30pm – 4:45pm: Tea Break 
4:45pm – 6:30pm: Whispers Of The Mountains
90 minutes | Rajasthani with English subtitles | 2025 | Jigar Nagda
Whispers Of The Mountains is a Rajasthani language drama directed by Jigar Nagda, featured in the Indian Panorama section of the 56th IFFI at Goa. It explores the fragile balance between ecological preservation and the livelihoods of communities living in the Aravalli region, underscoring the human cost of mining in Northwest India. 
The screening will be followed by an audience Q&A. 
6:30pm – 7pm: Closing Note

name: Self and Society
description:
This discussion examines the tension between personal autonomy and collective life, as explored across two novels, The Convert and Bhiku and His Bowl. In this moderated session, the two authors come together to reflect on what they see as a quiet loss of spirituality within modern communes, set against the growing dominance of organised religion, followed by questions from the audience. 
Both novels draw their ethical frameworks from native religious histories, treated not as systems of divine order but as moral architectures for imagining harmonious, communal life. Their relevance lies in their optimistic vision of secular eco-villages, spaces that continually negotiate individual expression against collective responsibility. They share the philosophical question: how much of the self must be yielded to a community in exchange for its survival, equity, and well-being, and how much spiritual search can remain a private, individual pursuit even within a shared life? What does it cost a self to belong to something larger than itself?

name: Malhar Barse: Where Clouds Meet Music
description:
The transformative beauty of rain is captured in the sounds of raga Malhar. While the 2009 concert gathered compositions whose lyrics evoked the monsoon’s imagery and mood, this morning turns inward, tracing the streams of raga Malhar itself: its many variants, melodic identities, and shifting character from the powerful and dramatic to the serene and contemplative. 
The performance moves through Miyan ki Malhar, Gaud Malhar, Megh Malhar, and others, each interpreted through khayal, tarana, bandish, and more. The programme also draws on bhajans and semi-classical compositions inspired by rain, tracing how Malhar’s essence has travelled across genres, connecting people through the magic of the monsoon: the anticipation before the rain, the romance of it, and the particular ache of longing that only this season seems to carry. The ensemble features Mowna Ramachandra on vocals, Sumit Naik on tabla, Tejas Katori on harmonium, and Supreetha Pradeep on tanpura. 
This performance is part of a series marking twenty years of BIC. It is a chance to trace what has changed, what has endured, and how ideas evolve over time. BIC is proud to have been host to conversations that connect culture, ideas, and public life across two decades.

name: Swarantar – A Mosaic of Melodies
description:
This concert explores twin ragas that differ by only a single swara, yet inhabit entirely different emotional worlds despite their near-identical scales. Presented side by side, the ragas reveal how one altered note reshapes melodic movement, how characteristic phrases diverge, and how the smallest shift in pitch can change a raga’s entire temperament. 
Ragas, the concert suggests, are not merely scales but living personalities. The comparative listening invites the audience into the mindset of composer and performer alike, showcasing the subtle moments where two melodic lines converge before parting to chart their own paths: a quiet reminder of the poetry hidden in what might otherwise pass unnoticed.

name: Berake Soppu
description:
Language: English and Kannada 
What if there is no such thing as a weed? This walking workshop challenges the very notion, exploring the uses, benefits, and precautions of foraging for wild edible greens growing in plain sight around us. 
In Kannada, berake soppu refers to a mix of wild greens traditionally foraged by women from fields, open spaces, and village commons, and cooked into nutritious dishes to feed their families. As store-bought greens and ready-made food become more available, the art of foraging, the skill of recognising wild edibles, and the traditional knowledge of cooking with them are slowly disappearing. Every plant has a role to play in its ecosystem, often one we have simply stopped noticing. 
Following a short introduction, participants will be guided through the neighbourhood to identify wild greens that go beyond the familiar palak, methi, or dhantu, learning their nutritional and traditional uses along the way. The walk closes with tea and further discussion, situating these plants within their wider social, cultural, and ecological significance. Learning to notice the greens underfoot, the session suggests, can change the way we see the landscape we move through every day.
